fixes.explanation: Not quite, friend. Lot, Abraham's nephew (Genesis 14:12), invites the two visitors to wash their feet and spend the night. They answer, “…we will spend the night in the square.” (Genesis 19:2) So their first answer is no, and it takes Lot insisting so strongly before they follow him into his house (Genesis 19:3).

That's it, friend. Lot, Abraham's nephew (Genesis 14:12), invites them in, and they answer, “…we will spend the night in the square.” (Genesis 19:2) They don't say yes right away. Lot has to insist so strongly that they finally follow him into his house (Genesis 19:3).

I see why a gift sounds right, friend, but the text doesn't mention one. It says Lot “…prepared a feast for them and baked unleavened bread, and they ate.” (Genesis 19:3) So it was a meal, and the guests ate it.

That's right, friend. “Lot went outside to meet them, shutting the door behind him.” (Genesis 19:6) He goes out to face the whole crowd, and his guests stay behind that door. Honestly, I'd have needed a minute and a cookie first. That's a lot of nerve.

The text never puts Lot on a roof, friend. It says he “…went outside to meet them, shutting the door behind him.” (Genesis 19:6) He goes out to them and shuts the door. That makes his next words even bolder.

Yes! “…the men inside reached out, pulled Lot into the house with them, and shut the door.” (Genesis 19:10) The crowd had just pressed in and moved to break down the door (Genesis 19:9). Lot gets pulled to safety right then. I'd like a friend who grabs me at exactly the right second.

A back way would be a smart plan, but the text never mentions one. It says the men inside “…reached out, pulled Lot into the house with them, and shut the door.” (Genesis 19:10) That's what happens: Lot is pulled in and the door is shut.

That's right, friend. The men inside “…struck the men at the entrance, young and old, with blindness, so that they wearied themselves trying to find the door.” (Genesis 19:11) A moment before, the crowd was moving in to break that door down (Genesis 19:9). Now all they can do is wear themselves out looking for it.

Sickness is a fair guess, but that's not what the text says. The men at the entrance were struck “…with blindness, so that they wearied themselves trying to find the door.” (Genesis 19:11) The text names blindness, and it's blindness that has them wearing themselves out looking for the door.

The crowd is a fair worry, friend, but it's not what the men say. Their reason is, “…we are about to destroy this place.” (Genesis 19:13) They say the outcry to the LORD against its people is so great that He has sent them to destroy it. Nothing in the text mentions the crowd coming back at dawn.

That's right, friend. “…his sons-in-law thought he was joking.” (Genesis 19:14) Lot has just told them the LORD is about to destroy the city. They hear a punchline instead of a warning. Tough crowd, and I know a thing or two about tough crowds.

Yes, friend. Lot says, “…there is a town nearby where I can flee, and it is a small place.” (Genesis 19:20) He asks to flee to that town instead of the mountains. Then he asks, “…is it not a small place?” and adds, “Then my life will be saved.”

Yes, friend. “…He remembered Abraham, and He brought Lot out of the catastrophe that destroyed the cities where he had lived.” (Genesis 19:29) Lot is Abraham's nephew (Genesis 14:12). Earlier, Abraham had spoken up to the LORD about Sodom (Genesis 18:23-32). The verse puts God remembering Abraham right beside Lot being brought out.

Sarah is Abraham's wife (Genesis 17:19), but this verse doesn't name her. It says, “…He remembered Abraham, and He brought Lot out of the catastrophe that destroyed the cities where he had lived.” (Genesis 19:29) So the name in the blank is Abraham. Lot is Abraham's nephew (Genesis 14:12).

Noah is from an earlier story, so that's a fair guess, friend. But this verse names someone else: “…He remembered Abraham, and He brought Lot out of the catastrophe that destroyed the cities where he had lived.” (Genesis 19:29) Lot is Abraham's nephew (Genesis 14:12). So the blank is Abraham.

The text doesn't say that, friend. It says Lot “…settled in the mountains—for he was afraid to stay in Zoar…” (Genesis 19:30) The reason it gives is that Lot was afraid to stay. It doesn't say anything about the town turning him away.
